text: The swan maiden is a folkloric figure of Ireland, Scotland, and the continent. She is a woman with a double nature, part human and part bird. At night she takes off her swan plumage and leaves it beside the lake where she swims. A man who finds the feather robe can make her his wife by hiding it. Then she stays, a hardworking helpmeet. If she ever finds her feathers again, she takes on bird form at once and flies away, leaving even her children behind. The tale is old. The bird carries religious meaning across Europe and appears among the Celts back to the Hallstatt period. The tale of Caer and Aonghus Og tells of two lovers who flew away together bound by a golden chain. A married swan woman often set rules on her man. The goddess Aine demanded that the Earl of Desmond show no surprise at anything their children did. When the rule broke, Aine and her son Geróid Iarla became waterbirds still seen on Lough Gur.
